[Metadata]

[Content]
Context
CC requires reliable, low-latency reasoning with predictable behavior. External APIs introduce variability in availability, cost, latency, and policy changes. Long-term autonomy and control require minimizing dependency on external services for core cognition.
Decision
Core reasoning and decision-making will run locally on CC’s machine. External APIs may be used only for non-core tasks such as optional enrichment or fallback capabilities.
Rationale
Local execution provides deterministic performance, full control over data, and independence from third-party constraints. While external APIs may offer stronger models at times, reliance on them for core reasoning introduces unacceptable operational and governance risk.
Alternatives Considered

Fully external reasoning via third-party APIs: rejected due to dependency and control risk.
Hybrid core reasoning split across local and external services: rejected due to complexity and unclear failure modes.

Success Criteria

CC performs core reasoning without requiring external API calls.
Reasoning latency remains within acceptable local hardware limits.
System continues to function during complete external network outages.

Rollback Plan
If local reasoning proves insufficient, temporarily re-enable external APIs for specific reasoning tasks while preserving local execution as the default path.
Notes
This decision assumes local hardware can support required model sizes. If hardware constraints change, a new ADR may be required.

Cache-Misses.title: Cache Misses
Cache-Misses.content:
Happen when the CPU looks for data in the cache but cannot find it there.
Main cases:


Cold miss (first access)
Happens when data is accessed for the first time. It has never been loaded into cache before.


Capacity miss
Happens when the cache is too small to hold all the data being used. Older data gets evicted, and when it is needed again, it is no longer there.


Conflict miss
Happens when multiple pieces of data map to the same cache location. Even if there is free space elsewhere, they replace each other due to how the cache is structured.


Coherence miss (multi-core systems)
Happens when another core modifies or invalidates a cached value, forcing a reload from main memory.


In short: cache misses occur when required data is not currently stored in the cache due to first-time access, limited size, mapping collisions, or multi-core updates.

Email-Evolution---Intent-Negotiation.title: Email Evolution - Intent Negotiation
Email-Evolution---Intent-Negotiation.content:
Good. This is one of the cleanest places where the break from old software becomes obvious.
Email and messaging exist because intent is lossy when passed through language. Words are a poor compression format for goals, constraints, priorities, uncertainty, and authority. Back-and-forth exists only to repair that loss.
Intent negotiation removes language as the primary carrier.
Here is how it works, structurally.
First, what replaces a message
A “message” becomes an intent object with explicit fields:


Goal: what must become true


Constraints: time, cost, quality, risk


Preferences: soft priorities


Authority: who can decide what


Uncertainty: what is unclear


Most of this is implicit today and inferred poorly by humans. AI makes it explicit by extracting it from natural input or behavior.
Second, what happens instead of sending
You do not send something to a person.
You submit intent into a shared negotiation space.
Each participant has:


Their own goals


Their own constraints


Their own authority bounds


The system computes overlap, conflict, and feasibility immediately.
Third, how alignment happens
Instead of replies, the system produces resolution states:


Aligned: goals compatible, no conflicts


Blocked: conflict exists, exact cause identified


Tradeoff required: list of viable compromises


Decision needed: identifies who must choose and why


Humans intervene only at true decision points, not during clarification.
Fourth, how “discussion” changes
Discussion becomes constraint adjustment, not conversation.
Examples:


Tightening a deadline automatically lowers quality expectations.


Increasing scope surfaces new blockers immediately.


Removing a constraint resolves three downstream conflicts at once.


No one argues. The system shows consequences.
Fifth, what disappears


Status updates (state is visible)


Follow-ups (open loops are explicit)


Misinterpretation (intent is structured)


Meetings for alignment (alignment is computed)


Sixth, what remains human


Value judgments


Risk tolerance


Taste


Final authority


The system does not decide what should matter.
It ensures everyone is reasoning about the same reality.
Why this feels radical
Email scales communication.
Intent negotiation scales coordination.
That is a deeper layer.

Evolving-Clarity.title: Evolving Clarity
Evolving-Clarity.content:
To evolve clarity means to make understanding sharper over time.
It is not about suddenly knowing everything. It is about repeatedly removing what is unnecessary, false, or vague until what remains is simple, accurate, and usable.
Clarity evolves as experience exposes mistakes, reflection corrects them, and attention narrows to what truly matters. What was once confusing becomes obvious, what was once noisy becomes quiet, and what was once complex becomes clean.
It is the movement from blurred perception to precise seeing, step by step.

Attractive distractions that look like they build clarity but actually prevent it:
Consuming information without deciding anything. Reading, watching, and listening feel productive, but if no decision or stance follows, clarity does not increase. It only delays commitment.
Refining language instead of refining thought. Renaming ideas, polishing frameworks, or finding better words can mask the fact that the core understanding is still weak.
Seeking certainty before acting. Waiting until something feels fully clear keeps clarity frozen. Real clarity often appears only after contact with reality.
Collecting multiple perspectives endlessly. Exposure feels broad-minded, but clarity comes from selecting one lens and testing it, not from holding many at once.
Building systems instead of answering the real question. Tools, notes, workflows, and structures can become substitutes for confronting what you actually believe or want.
Mistaking complexity for depth. Adding layers, nuance, and exceptions can feel intelligent while quietly avoiding a simple, uncomfortable truth.
Revisiting the same question without changing conditions. Thinking again and again without new action, input, or constraint produces the illusion of progress.
These behaviors feel aligned with evolving clarity, but they preserve ambiguity rather than dissolve it.

Master-Artificial-Intelligence.title: Master Artificial Intelligence
Master-Artificial-Intelligence.content:
To master AI means having reliable control over what AI produces, when it produces it, and why it produces it.
It includes understanding how to frame intent clearly so the system responds predictably, knowing the limits and biases of the tool so you are not misled by it, and being able to turn vague goals into precise outcomes using language, structure, and judgment.
Mastery is not about knowing how AI works internally. It is about using it deliberately, correcting it quickly, and integrating it into thinking and execution so it amplifies your ability rather than replaces it.
It is about the AI as an actor you interact with, not as a machine you engineer.
What matters is how intention passes through language, constraints, context, timing, and feedback, and emerges as usable action.
In that sense, AI is closer to an instrument than a mechanism. Mastery is knowing how it responds to pressure, ambiguity, precision, silence, correction, and framing. Two people can use the same system and get radically different power from it. The difference is not technical knowledge, but control.
It lives at a higher level: the level of agency, leverage, and coordination between human judgment and artificial capability.

The most dangerous distractions are the ones that feel like progress.
First: obsessing over internals, terminology, or theory that never changes how you use the system. Learning how models are trained, named, or compared can feel like mastery, but it rarely improves control, outcomes, or leverage. It satisfies curiosity, not capability.
Second: prompt hoarding and prompt aesthetics. Collecting clever prompts, templates, or “magic phrases” looks productive, but it externalizes thinking. Mastery comes from adapting intent in real time, not from reusing artifacts created by others or by your past self.
Third: chasing novelty. New models, new tools, new features, new benchmarks. This creates motion without depth. Switching contexts prevents you from learning how one system actually behaves under pressure, ambiguity, or failure.
Fourth: treating AI as an oracle instead of a collaborator. Asking for answers instead of shaping processes. When you rely on outputs without interrogating, correcting, or redirecting them, you lose agency and mistake convenience for control.
Fifth: over-automation before understanding. Delegating tasks you do not yet understand creates the illusion of efficiency while eroding judgment. You cannot master what you cannot evaluate.
Sixth: measuring progress by volume. More prompts, more chats, more generated content. Quantity feels like momentum, but mastery is visible in fewer interactions producing more precise results.
These are attractive because they are easy, measurable, and socially validated. None of them increase your command over AI behavior. They only make you feel closer to it.

New software paradigms. Not just better code, but new programming models, abstractions, and execution styles humans would not design. These are currently theoretical because evaluating an entirely new paradigm requires years of tooling, benchmarks, and ecosystem building. A self-improving system can create, test, discard, and evolve paradigms internally.
Self-evolving objectives. Goals stop being fixed. The system can examine its own values, detect internal contradictions, and refine them while remaining coherent. This is currently theoretical because goal drift is treated as failure. Self-improvement allows the system to redesign the concept of alignment itself.
Automatic discovery of “unknown unknowns.” The system identifies entire categories of questions humans never ask, not by extrapolation, but by detecting gaps in conceptual space. This is theoretical because humans define the problem spaces. Self-improving software can redefine the space itself.
Reversible intelligence. The system can deliberately simplify itself, forget capabilities, or regress to earlier cognitive forms to explore alternative evolutionary paths, then reassemble what was useful. This is impossible today because loss of capability is treated as irreversible damage.
Reality interface design. Instead of modeling the world, the system designs how the world should be measured—what sensors, abstractions, and feedback loops should exist—then builds cognition around that. This inverts the usual order of perception then intelligence. It is theoretical because perception is treated as fixed.
Thought-speed civilization. Entire economies, cultures, and scientific communities exist purely inside accelerated cognition, interacting with the physical world only at decision boundaries. → this is something I can do and use now (the italicize)

Sometimes it just silently reads files for 10, 15 minutes before starting to write any code.


just say “let’s discuss” as part of your prompt


I simply start a conversation with the model, ask a question, let it google, explore code, create a plan together, and when I’m happy with what I see, I write “build” or “write plan to docs/*.md and build this”


I also wanted to give him the ability to check on my agents, and getting a character stream is just far more efficient than looking at images… if this will work out, we’ll see!


 When you do enough agentic engineering, you develop a feeling for what’s gonna be easy and where the model likely will struggle, so often I just put in a prompt, codex will chug along for 30 minutes and I have what I need.


Sometimes it takes a little fiddling or creativity, but often things are straightforward.


I extensively use the queueing feature of codex - as I get a new idea, I add it to the pipeline.


My approach to building software is very iterative. I build sth, play with it, see how it “feels”, and then get new ideas to refine it.


Rarely do I have a complete picture of what I want in my head.


So systems that take the complete idea as input and then deliver output wouldn’t work well for me.


I need to play with it, touch it, feel it, see it, that’s how I evolve it.


I basically never revert or use checkpointing.


I simply commit to main. 


I find the added cognitive load of having to think of different states in my projects unnecessary and prefer to evolve it linearly. 


I’ve already mentioned my way of planning a feature. I cross-reference projects all the time, esp if I know that I already solved sth somewhere else, I ask codex to look in ../project-folder and that’s usually enough for it to infer from context where to look. This is extremely useful to save on prompts. I can just write “look at ../vibetunnel and do the same for Sparkle changelogs”, because it’s already solved there and with a 99% guarantee it’ll correctly copy things over and adapt to the new project. That’s how I scaffold new projects as well.


I’ve seen plenty of systems for folks wanting to refer to past sessions. Another thing I never need or use. I maintain docs for subsystems and features in a docs folder in each project, and use a script + some instructions in my global AGENTS file to force the model to read docs on certain topics. This pays off more the larger the project is, so I don’t use it everywhere, but it is of great help to keep docs up-to-date and engineer a better context for my tasks.


Apropos context. I used to be really diligent to restart a session for new tasks. With GPT 5.2 this is no longer needed. Performance is extremely good even when the context is fuller, and often it helps with speed since the model works faster when it already has loaded plenty files. Obviously that only works well when you serialize your tasks or keep the changes so far apart that two sessions don’t touch each other much. 


Prompts. I used to write long, elaborate prompts with voice dictation. With codex, my prompts gotten much shorter, I often type again, and many times I add images, especially when iterating on UI (or text copies with CLIs). If you show the model what’s wrong, just a few words are enough to make it do what you want. Yes, I’m that person that drags in a clipped image of some UI component with “fix padding” or “redesign”, many times that either solves my issue or gets me reasonably far. I used to refer to markdown files, but with my docs:list script that’s no longer necessary.


Markdowns. Many times I write “write docs to docs/*.md” and simply let the model pick a filename. The more obvious you design the structure for what the model is trained on, the easier your work will be. After all, I don’t design codebases to be easy to navigate for me, I engineer them so agents can work in it efficiently. Fighting the model is often a waste of time and tokens.


What’s still hard? Picking the right dependency and framework to set on is something I invest quite some time on. Is this well-maintained? How about peer dependencies? Is it popular = will have enough world knowledge so agents have an easy time? Equally, system design. Will we communicate via web sockets? HTML? What do I put into the server and what into the client? How and which data flows where to where? Often these are things that are a bit harder to explain to a model and where research and thinking pays off.


Since I manage lots of projects, often I let an agent simply run in my project folder and when I figure out a new pattern, I ask it to “find all my recent go projects and implement this change there too + update changelog”. 


Ofc I automate everything. There’s a skill to register domains and change DNS. One to write good frontends. There’s a note in my AGENTS file about my tailscale network so I can just say “go to my mac studio and update xxx”.


I usually work on two Macs. My MacBook Pro on the big screen, and a Jump Desktop session to my Mac Studio on another screen. Some projects are cooking there, some here. Sometimes I edit different parts of the same project on each machine and sync via git. Simpler than worktrees because drifts on main are easy to reconcile. Has the added benefit that anything that needs UI or browser automation I can move to my Studio and it won’t annoy me with popups.


I used to play with slash commands, but just never found them too useful. Skills replaced some of it, and for the rest I keep writing “commit/push” because it takes the same time as /commit and always works.


In the past I often took dedicated days to refactor and clean up projects, I do this much more ad-hoc now. Whenever prompts start taking too long or I see sth ugly flying by in the code stream, I’ll deal with it right away.


I tried linear or other issue trackers, but nothing did stick. Important ideas I try right away, and everything else I’ll either remember or it wasn’t important. Of course I have public bug trackers for bugs for folks that use my open source code, but when I find a bug, I’ll immediately prompt it - much faster than writing it down and then later having to switch context back to it.


Whatever you build, start with the model and a CLI first.


My go-to model is gpt-5.2-codex high. Again, KISS. There’s very little benefit to xhigh other than it being far slower, and I don’t wanna spend time thinking about different modes or “ultrathink”. So pretty much everything runs on high. GPT 5.2 and codex are close enough that changing models makes no sense, so I just use that.

Unix-Commands-Forms-in-the-AI-Era.content:
The next evolution is not “AI versions” of those companies. It is a different axis entirely.
Unix → startups mapped commands → services.
AI maps intent → outcome.
Below are the true successors, framed as primitives, not products. Each line is one evolutionary jump, with several concrete idea shapes.

Search (grep → Google)
Next: Truth synthesis


Ask a question and receive a structured answer that explains itself, cites sources, and adapts as facts change.


Continuous beliefs that update over time instead of static search results.


Personal truth layers: the same question answered differently based on your goals, risk tolerance, or context.



File sync (rsync → Dropbox)
🤔 Next: State continuity


You never manage files; your work state follows you across devices and moments.


Thought-level versioning: not “files,” but decisions, drafts, and intentions are synced.


Roll back meaning, not bytes.



Scheduling (cron)
Next: Autonomous time allocation


You express outcomes; the system rearranges time automatically.


Deadlines negotiate with each other.


Time becomes elastic, not blocked.



Monitoring (top, ps → Datadog)
🤔 Next: Self-explaining systems


Systems narrate what they are doing and why.


Failures are explained before they are noticed.


Monitoring shifts from watching metrics to understanding behavior.



Version control (diff → GitHub)
🤔 Next: Decision lineage


Every choice has a traceable history: why it was made, what alternatives existed, what changed.


Teams fork decisions, not code.


Undo regret, not commits.



Remote access (ssh → cloud platforms)
Next: Capability delegation
🤔 - You don’t access machines; you delegate intent.

“Make this true” replaces “log into this box.”

🤔 - Resources assemble themselves temporarily to fulfill a request, then disappear.

Build systems (make, CI)
Next: Outcome compilation


You describe what success looks like; the system figures out the steps.


Pipelines are inferred, not written.


🤔 - Failure produces revised plans, not error logs.

Email / messaging (mail)  Email Evolution - Intent Negotiation
🤔 Next: Intent negotiation
🤔 - Messages are replaced by goals and constraints.
🤔 - Back-and-forth disappears; alignment happens instantly.
🤔 - Communication shifts from words to shared understanding.

Databases
Next: Living memory


Data reorganizes itself based on use.


Queries change the structure.


Memory becomes active, not stored.



UI / dashboards
Next: Disappearing interfaces


No menus, no flows, no screens as the primary object.


The interface is conversation, gesture, or silence.


Visibility only appears when uncertainty exists.



The unifying shift:
Old software answered: “Which tool do you want?”
SaaS answered: “Which workflow fits you?”
AI answers: “What do you want to be true?”
That is why SaaS feels outdated to you. It still lives one layer too low.

05_Archive/Outcome-Aligned-File-Naming-C.title: Outcome-Aligned File Naming Convention
05_Archive/Outcome-Aligned-File-Naming-C.content:
A file name exists to state why the file must exist for its outcome to become true.
If the name does not answer that, the file is incorrectly named.
A file name should answer one question only: what role does this file play in making the outcome true.

Core structure
<intent>__<role>[__<scope>].<ext>
• intent describes the state change the file causes
• role explains the function the file serves
• scope is optional and only used to clarify boundaries
• the extension is purely technical and ignored conceptually
Double underscores separate meaning, not hierarchy.

1) Intent rule
Intent is written as a verb phrase that moves the outcome forward.
Use verbs that imply change or enforcement, not activity.
If the file does not clearly push the outcome toward “true,” it does not belong.
Correct:
define, decide, enforce, ensure, measure, validate, trigger
Incorrect:
write, build, test, draft
Example:
decide__task_prioritization.md

2) Role rule
The role states what the file does, not what it contains or how it is implemented.
Ask: “What would stop working if this file disappeared?”
Correct roles:
criteria, policy, signal, memory, contract, evaluator, schedule
Incorrect roles:
notes, utils, script, final, v2
Example:
enforce__planning_constraints.yaml

3) One reason to exist
Each file serves exactly one reason for the outcome.
If a file exists for multiple reasons, it must be split.
Correct:
measure__execution_signal.py
Incorrect:
planning_and_execution.py

4) Outcome-bound rule
If the outcome is true, the file should still matter.
Process artifacts do not belong.
Correct:
ensure__context_continuity.memory
Incorrect:
early_ideas.md, experiment_3.py

5) Scope rule (optional)
Scope is used only to distinguish meaning, never time, order, or version.
Correct:
enforce__constraints__daily.yaml
enforce__constraints__long_term.yaml
Incorrect:
constraints_final.yaml, constraints_2026.yaml

6) Special rule for prompts
Files whose primary function is to be consumed as prompts MUST end with __prompt, regardless of extension.
This suffix is semantic, not technical.
Prompt files follow:
<intent>__<role>[__<scope>]__prompt.<ext>
Examples:
decide__task_prioritization__prompt.md
generate__daily_plan__prompt.txt
evaluate__plan_quality__prompt.md
Non-prompt files must not use this suffix.

7) Self-legibility requirement
The filesystem must explain the system without external context.
A reader should infer the logic of the outcome by reading file names alone.
Correct set:
define__success_criteria.md
decide__task_prioritization__prompt.md
enforce__planning_constraints.yaml
measure__execution_signal.py
validate__plan_coherence.py
Incorrect set:
notes.md
utils.py
script_v4.py

Examples
Examples within an outcome like “CC Autonomous Daily Planning”:
• define__success_criteria.md
• enforce__planning_constraints.yaml
• decide__task_prioritization__prompt.md
• measure__plan_execution_signal.py
• ensure__context_continuity.memory
• validate__daily_plan_coherence.py
• trigger__planning_cycle.schedule
None of these names care how they are implemented. Only why they exist.

This turns the filesystem into a truth table for CC’s progress, where directories assert what should exist, and files assert why each piece exists.

05_Archive/Outcome-Driven-Directory-Stru.title: Outcome-Driven Directory Structure
05_Archive/Outcome-Driven-Directory-Stru.content:
An outcome-driven directory structure is organized by outcomes, not by technology, layer, or function.
It treats the filesystem as a map of intent, not implementation.
An outcome is a concrete state change intended to exist in the world if the work succeeds. Every top-level directory represents exactly one outcome and is named after that outcome.

Directories
Top-level directories must be named as outcomes, not tasks, tools, or abstractions. Names describe an achieved state, not an activity. If the outcome no longer matters, the entire directory can be archived without affecting others.
Each root directory answers one question only: what is supposed to exist in the world if this succeeds.
Examples (good directory names):
• Acquire First 100 Users
• Enable CC Daily Autonomous Planning
• Generate Weekly Business Insights
• Reduce User Onboarding Friction
• Launch Public CC Beta
• Automate Personal Knowledge Capture
These names describe a concrete outcome or state change. If completed, the name would read as true.
A state change name encodes a before and after. CC can always tell whether the directory is “true” or “false.”
Counter-examples (bad directory names):
• Marketing
• AI Agent
• Planning System
• Backend
• Experiments
• Prompts
• Analytics Tools
These describe functions, components, or domains rather than outcomes. They do not imply completion or success and therefore fail as outcome roots.

Contents
Everything inside an outcome directory exists solely to serve that outcome. If a file cannot clearly justify its contribution to the outcome named at the root, it does not belong there.
Code, prompts, data, experiments, notes, and automation live together because they share a single reason to exist.
There is no fixed internal directory structure. Internal structure is allowed to emerge organically and may differ between outcomes. Subdirectories are created only when repetition or scale makes them unavoidable.
File naming is strict and carries meaning independently of location.
Files must remain understandable when viewed, copied, searched, or generated in isolation. Meaning must not rely on directory position.

Directory is fragile, file naming is robust.
Directories express  groupings, filenames express identity and role.
Identity survives change; grouping does not.
Structure is deferred, not denied. Patterns that consistently emerge across multiple outcomes may later be standardized, but never in advance.
This rule prioritizes intent clarity, mobility, and long-term coherence over premature order.

100_Canonical/ADR-v1---Metadata.title: ADR v1 - Metadata
100_Canonical/ADR-v1---Metadata.content:
adr-id
A unique, permanent identifier for this decision record.
It must never be reused or changed.
Its purpose is stable referencing and traceability across time.

adr-version
The version of the ADR schema and governance rules in effect when this ADR was created.
It does not describe the decision itself and must not change after creation.
It is used to correctly interpret metadata semantics in the future.

created-at
The exact timestamp when the ADR was first created.
It represents when the decision was proposed, not when it was approved or implemented.

status
The current lifecycle state of the decision.


proposed
The decision is suggested but not yet approved.


approved
The decision is authorized but not yet executed.


implemented
The decision has been executed and is in effect.


rejected
The decision was formally evaluated and explicitly declined.
When an ADR is marked as rejected, a human-authored reasoning explaining why the decision was rejected must be added to the ADR content.


deprecated
The decision is no longer recommended but may still be in use.
When an ADR is marked as deprecated, a reasoning explaining why the decision is no longer preferred must be added to the ADR content.


superseded
The decision has been explicitly replaced by another ADR.
When an ADR is marked as superseded, a reasoning explaining the replacement and references to the superseding ADR(s) must be added to the ADR content.



proposer
Identifies who initiated the decision.


cc
The decision was proposed autonomously by CC.


H
The decision was proposed by H.



urgency
Describes how time-sensitive the decision is, independent of risk.


high
Delay will cause immediate or near-term degradation, blockage, or loss of capability.


medium
Delay is acceptable for a limited time; acting sooner improves outcomes but is not critical.


low
No time pressure; postponement has no negative impact.



risk-level
Describes the likelihood and severity of negative outcomes if the change fails.


high
Failure can cause loss of control, security exposure, irreversible damage, or inability to recover.


medium
Failure can degrade core functionality but does not threaten overall recoverability.


low
Failure affects non-core behavior and is contained and recoverable.


negligible
Failure has no meaningful impact beyond minor inconvenience.



change-domain
Describes which part of CC is primarily affected by the decision.
This list is extensible.


skill
Adds or modifies a specific capability.


model
Changes the AI model or inference behavior.


software
Installs, removes, or modifies external tools.


system
Alters core architecture or permissions.


policy
Changes governing rules or constraints.


memory
Alters information storage or retrieval.



impact-scope
Describes how broadly the change affects CC.


local
The change affects a single, isolated component.


system-wide
The change affects core mechanisms or multiple components.



reversibility
Describes the ability to undo the change and restore the prior state.


reversible
Full restoration is possible with no loss.


partially-reversible
Functional restoration is possible with some loss.


irreversible
The prior state cannot be restored.



related-adrs
A list of ADR identifiers that are contextually linked to this decision, such as dependencies or superseded records.

100_Canonical/ADR-v1---Schema.title: ADR v1 - Schema
100_Canonical/ADR-v1---Schema.content:
Metadata:
adr-id: ADR-XXXX
adr-version: X
created-at: YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm
status: proposed | approved | implemented | deprecated | superseded
proposer: CC | H
urgency: high | medium | low
risk-level: high | medium | low | negligible
change-domain: skill | model | software | system | policy | memory
impact-scope: local | system-wide
reversibility: reversible | partially-reversible | irreversible
related-adrs: [ADR-XXXX, ADR-YYYY]
Content:
Context
Describe the situation, constraints, and conditions that led to this decision.
State facts only. No conclusions or preferences.
Decision
State exactly what is being changed, added, removed, or adopted.
This section must be unambiguous and executable.
Rationale
Explain why this decision was chosen over alternatives.
Include assumptions, tradeoffs, and reasoning used at the time.
If the selected urgency or risk-level is non-obvious or counterintuitive, the reasoning must be explained here.  s
Alternatives Considered
List other viable options that were available, including why they were not chosen.
Success Criteria
Define concrete, observable conditions that determine whether the decision is successful.
Rollback Plan
Describe how to revert or mitigate the change if success criteria are not met.
Rejection Reasoning (required if status = rejected)
Explain why the decision was declined.
This reasoning must be human-authored and explicit.
Deprecation Reasoning (required if status = deprecated)
Explain why the decision is no longer preferred and under what conditions it remains in use, if any.
Supersession Reasoning (required if status = superseded)
Explain why this decision was replaced and reference the ADR(s) that supersede it.
Notes
Record additional assumptions, constraints, or future considerations that do not fit elsewhere.

100_Canonical/ADR-v1---Title-Rule.title: ADR v1 - Title Rule
100_Canonical/ADR-v1---Title-Rule.content:
An ADR title must be a single declarative sentence that states the final architectural decision in clear, concrete terms.
Core requirements

State what is being adopted, enforced, added, removed, or replaced
Use a verb that implies execution or commitment
Refer to a system domain or capability, not a vague concept
The title must still be unambiguous when read alone in a list
Explicitly include what is chosen and what is rejected
Do not describe intent, exploration, or process

Contrast requirement

If the decision explicitly forbids, replaces, or constrains a viable alternative, the rejected option must be named in the title using a clear contrast (e.g., “not”, “instead of”, “replacing”)
If the decision is purely additive or enabling, do not invent a contrast

Examples

Run Core Reasoning Locally, Not via External APIs
Replace Heuristic Planning with Model-Based Planning
Add Vision Capability to CC
Introduce Structured Memory for User Preferences

100_Canonical/Tags-vs-Metadata.title: Tags vs Metadata
100_Canonical/Tags-vs-Metadata.content:
Metadata / Front-matter:

Use metadata for machine decisions
Use when the information should change AI behavior or be parsed deterministically
Metadata is in singular form

Tags:

100_Canonical/Writing.title: Writing
100_Canonical/Writing.content:
Explicit Over Implicit
Write what you mean. Do not rely on context, memory, or implied references.
Structure Beats Style
Prefer simple structure over expressive writing.
Timeless Language When Possible
Avoid time-bound phrases like “recently,” “now,” or “these days” unless time is the subject.
This keeps notes valid for long-term AI reasoning.
Second-Person
You mostly write for yourself, talk to yourself directly by using “you”.
Use Proper Grammar and Punctuations
This reduces ambiguity, improves parsing by humans and machines, and preserves meaning without requiring interpretation.

90_Definitions/Active-Note.title: Active Note
90_Definitions/Active-Note.content:
A note located at the root of the vault.
It represents current thinking and is assumed to be editable, provisional, and operational.

90_Definitions/Architecture-Decision-Rec.title: Architecture Decision Records (ADR)
90_Definitions/Architecture-Decision-Rec.content:
The purpose of ADRs is memory and clarity.
They explain why the system is the way it is, not just what it is.
This helps to understand past tradeoffs without relying on oral history or guesswork.
ADRs preserve reason, not just outcomes.
ADRs are not just architectural memory; they are governance artifacts for CC’s self-directed evolution.
Each ADR captures a single architectural decision together with the context, reasoning, and consequences necessary to understand and evaluate that decision in the future.

90_Definitions/CC.title: CC
90_Definitions/CC.content:
H’s ultimate AI assistant.
Extremely adaptable.
“All problems can be solved with AI and human collaboration”
“CC” as a name, has a very deep meaning to H.
CC is exactly derived from C.C. of Code Geass.
H wishes if he had a personal ultimate assistant, she hoped it would be deeply comparable to C.C. and that reason is why he is creating CC.

90_Definitions/Canonical-Note.title: Canonical Note
90_Definitions/Canonical-Note.content:
A note stored under 100_Canonical.
It represents authoritative, long-lived knowledge.
Its content is treated as higher priority than Active or Legacy notes.
Canonical Notes are edited deliberately and infrequently.
Canonical Notes are the final form of thought in your system.
They are not where thinking happens. They are where thinking ends.
A Canonical Note represents something you are willing to treat as true, stable, and reusable across time.

90_Definitions/Definition-Note.title: Definition Note
90_Definitions/Definition-Note.content:
A note stored under 90_Definitions.
It contains stable semantic anchors that define the precise meaning of terms used across the system.
Definitions clarify language and prevent conceptual drift, but do not prescribe behavior or enforce structure.
Notes in this directory are authoritative in meaning, edited infrequently, and referenced broadly.
When a definition begins to impose constraints or govern behavior, it no longer belongs here and must be promoted to Canonical as a rule.

90_Definitions/H.title: H
90_Definitions/H.content:
CC’s creator.
A human who decided to fully integrate most of his life to artificial intelligence.
A human who are not gifted of exceptional intelligence, elite talents, and wealth but aims to be one of the great men in his generation.

90_Definitions/Legacy-Note.title: Legacy Note
90_Definitions/Legacy-Note.content:
A note stored under 00_Legacy.
It represents historical thinking and is treated as read-only context.

90_Definitions/Question-Note.title: Question Note
90_Definitions/Question-Note.content:
A note stored under 10_Questions.
It represents an unresolved inquiry or uncertainty that is currently occupying attention.
Its content is minimal, scoped to a single topic with just enough context to make the question precise.
Question Notes are temporary by nature and exist to be resolved, not expanded.
When answered, their substance is either promoted into an Active or Canonical note, and the Question Note is removed.

_os/SETUP.title: How to run this locally
_os/SETUP.content:
The vault is pre-configured to render as a navigable site with Quartz — backlinks, graph view, clickable wikilinks, full-text search. About 3 minutes to run, one-time.
Prerequisites

Space is crowded: CrewAI, LangGraph, AutoGen, OpenAI’s Swarm, a dozen others.

Your real edge is one layer up: taste + philosophy + lived practice of running a personal AI assistant. Nearly uncontested. Maps directly onto Kaizen Mechanism, CC - Foundational Setup Ideas, and Evolving Clarity.

I parked the swarm in kill-list with the reasoning. If someone else is waiting on it, let them. If you still want to pursue it, go in with the market read.

Writer-builder path. Appleton / Gwern / Ness Labs archetype. Publish the vault as a navigable site, write one flagship essay (“Clarity is the new limit” is already sitting there), ship an opinionated starter kit people can fork. _os/hiro-profile.title: A read of Hiro from outside
_os/hiro-profile.content:
An outside read, written after an afternoon in the vault. Sourced to specific notes throughout. Argue with anything that’s wrong.
What Hiro is
A design engineer. His public portfolio says so explicitly: hirosl on GitHub is described as “A personal portfolio site as a design engineer.” The repos he has shipped publicly are design-adjacent: design-observations (a blog about design), portfolio.design-observations, we-work-with-ai (a curated AI jobs board), context-aware-webinar, crocro (a private real-time chat browser extension). Small, intentional, aesthetic. Zero stars across all of them. He has not yet shipped anything publicly at the scale his thinking suggests he could.
A power user of OpenClaw. The vault contains OpenClaw Release Notes.md (a tracking note) and Income Ideas.md references his “OC” instance (“A wrapper that sends requests to my OC”). OpenClaw is Peter Steinberger’s personal-AI-assistant project — 356k GitHub stars, TypeScript, multi-platform. Hiro is not on the contributor list. He is a thoughtful reader/user who has written his own design-level opinions on top of it. CC in the vault is Hiro’s personal instance of OpenClaw (or an OpenClaw-like setup), named after C.C. from Code Geass, configured according to his own philosophy.
A careful writer who thinks in aphorisms. 100_Canonical/Writing.md gives his own rules: “Explicit over implicit. Structure beats style. Timeless language when possible. Second-person. Use proper grammar and punctuations.” His best sentences are quotable — “The new limit is clarity,” “Think in outcomes, not steps,” “Learn only what you will use imminently.” He writes like someone who is building a personal operating system out of maxims.
An introspective person under real pressure. Self-Observation.md contains entries that make clear he does his best work from equanimity, not from pressure, and is currently dealing with people in his life who drain him. Specific lines: “I really find it hard to [work under pressure] … I always do my best thinking and action when I am on the state of equanimity,” and “I need to decide to stop,” and a long passage about entities that pull him down. This is personal, not professional, and it shapes every recommendation in this folder.
What Hiro is not

Not a backend/infrastructure engineer. The vault has zero code, zero architecture diagrams (outside one Excalidraw), zero system specs written in the voice of someone who has designed distributed systems.
Not the author of an existing shippable product. OpenClaw is Peter Steinberger’s. The quotes in Shipping at Inference Speed - Pointers.md are Steinberger’s blog post, not Hiro’s. This is worth stating plainly because it affects how any product pitch is framed.
Not a high-volume shipper. His public repos are few, small, and quiet. This is a characteristic, not a flaw — but it means the product strategy cannot assume “ship a framework and watch it go viral.”
Not somebody who will thrive in a venture sprint. H - Prime explicitly values “works minimally, AI does the rest, only judgment and highest-impact decisions are made. Study most of the time. Exercise. Do things he love or with his loved ones.” That is not the self-model of someone who wants to run a 60-hour-week startup.
Not somebody who wants public attention for its own sake. His GitHub follower count is 1. His profile has no bio, no blog link, no twitter. He is deliberately low-profile.

What Hiro’s distinctive edge actually is
After the above, what’s left is the real asset, and it’s big:

A genuinely unusual first-principles point of view on what personal AI assistants should feel like. Not “what should they do” (the whole industry talks about that) but “how should they feel, align, compound, fail gracefully, earn trust.” This is the design question, not the engineering question, and almost nobody with good taste is writing about it publicly.
Design-engineer taste applied to AI tooling. He notices what is ugly and what is clean. He cares about structure. He wrote canonical rules about note-taking and insisted on ADRs for his own AI assistant’s behavior. This taste, externalized, is a product.
A working personal AI setup that embodies a philosophy. CC is a real thing he runs. The Kaizen Mechanism.md is a real spec he wrote for how that thing should get better at working with him. Whether or not anyone else sees it, it exists. That’s a working prototype of a point of view.
The quiet credibility of someone who was clearly going to build this anyway. Hiro is not writing the vault because it’s a content strategy. He is writing it because his own mind needs it. That’s legible to readers, and it is the hardest kind of credibility to fake.

The shape of a path forward
The combination above — design engineer + aesthetic point of view + a running personal setup + aversion to the spotlight + the need for equanimity — points, clearly, at a very specific kind of career move.
It is not “ship a startup.”
It is closer to: become the quiet, trusted author of the design philosophy for personal AI assistants. Writing first, templates second, opinionated starter kits third, paid products fourth. Possibly, in the long run, a book. The model is Maggie Appleton / Gwern / Nadia Asparouhova / the early Ness Labs era — writer-builders with strong aesthetics whose work compounds slowly and then unreasonably, without any of them having to do the Twitter performance.
The distinctive thing Hiro can do that Appleton/Gwern/etc. cannot is operate from inside a running personal AI system he’s designed himself. That grounds the writing and makes every essay a field report instead of a think piece. That’s the wedge.
What this profile is not
Not a business plan. Not a diagnosis. Not advice. An outside read, put in writing so Hiro can mark up where it’s wrong. Mark it up.

_os/product/prototype.title: What v0 actually looks like
_os/product/prototype.content:
Four concrete artifacts, sketched. Not a real implementation — a drawing of what the real thing could be, enough for Hiro to react to.
1. The rendered vault — a walk through someone’s mind
Stack: Quartz v4. Free, open source, designed for exactly this (Obsidian vault → static site with working wikilinks, backlinks, graph view, tags, full-text search). Deployable to GitHub Pages in ~15 minutes.
What the homepage says (approximate):
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Hiro                                            │
│                                                  │
│  notes on running a personal AI assistant.      │
│  unfinished on purpose. come in and walk.       │
│                                                  │
│  start anywhere:                                 │
│   → clarity is the new limit                    │
│   → the kaizen loop                             │
│   → what CC is                                   │
│   → the canonical rules                          │
│                                                  │
│  all notes · graph · tags · search              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Minimal. Serif or monospace headline. One column. The graph view sits in the corner, live, clickable. Backlinks automatic. No navigation bar beyond the essentials.
The feeling we want: you opened a door, it’s dim, the walls are books. You can read any book, but you didn’t have to pay to walk in, and the writing is clearly alive.
What this is not: a blog. A blog implies curation, a queue, polish. This is a vault — the raw notebook of somebody thinking in public. The unfinished-ness is a feature. Readers who get it will tell other readers.
2. The flagship essay — “Clarity is the new limit”
~1200 words. Published on a clean personal domain (probably just hiro.xyz or similar) or a Substack. Under Hiro’s first name only.
Rough structure (draft in later passes):

Hook: Hiro’s own line, verbatim or close: “The new limit is clarity.” Not about models. Not about speed. About the thing that bottlenecks everything now that the models are good enough.
Reframe: the old limits were muscle and time. Then compute and expertise. Now it’s how clearly you can say what you mean. The AI isn’t the bottleneck anymore. You are.
Where clarity shows up in practice: three scenes. (a) A CLAUDE.md file that is 90% right and 10% vague, and the 10% is why the agent keeps misfiring. (b) A team meeting that is 45 minutes long because nobody wrote down what they actually wanted before it started. (c) A person who is “busy” but cannot answer what their current project is for.
Why everyone gets this wrong: they optimize for per-task output. Faster prompts, faster code, faster commits. This is optimizing the wrong loop. The compounding loop is clarity → better instructions → better compounding, and it is invisible unless you look for it.
The practice: a daily or per-session Kaizen loop. Pulled directly from Kaizen Mechanism.md. The assistant reports what blocked it, what was ambiguous, what should change. The human reviews. The system compounds. This is Hiro’s actual practice, and it grounds every abstract claim.
Close: short. “The amount of software you can ship is now limited only by how clearly you can say what you want. If your setup isn’t helping you clarify, your setup is the thing you’re not clear about yet.”

Voice rules for this draft pass:

Use Hiro’s actual phrases from the vault wherever possible.
Second-person. His canonical Writing.md says so: “You mostly write for yourself, talk to yourself directly by using ‘you’.”
Short paragraphs. No more than three sentences per paragraph anywhere.
No lists in the body. This is an essay, not a guide.
Quote nobody else. Don’t name-drop. The voice is the point.

3. The CC Starter Kit — “a recipe, not a framework”
Form: a GitHub repo, MIT-licensed, small. Anybody can fork it, open it in their editor, and follow a 60-second setup.
Contents of the repo (rough):
cc-starter-kit/
├── README.md                  — "install in 60 seconds" + philosophy blurb
├── CLAUDE.md.template         — the starter CLAUDE.md, with comments
│                                explaining each section and inviting
│                                the user to edit it
├── skills/
│   ├── reflect-on-session.md  — triggered at end of session,
│   │                             asks agent: "what blocked you?
│   │                             what should change about your instructions?"
│   ├── propose-improvements.md — parses reflection into concrete diffs
│   ├── distill-memory.md      — moves durable lessons from session
│   │                             notes into CLAUDE.md
│   └── README.md              — when to use each, how to customize
├── hooks/
│   └── stop.sh                — Claude Code Stop hook that triggers
│                                the reflection skill automatically
├── docs/
│   ├── philosophy.md          — the "why" in 500 words
│   ├── the-kaizen-loop.md     — how the reflection → distill
│   │                             → instruction loop works in practice
│   ├── what-goes-where.md     — memory vs skills vs hooks vs docs:
│   │                             the taste question
│   └── first-week.md          — what to do the first week after
│                                 installing, to actually get value
└── examples/
    ├── example-session.md     — a real (or realistic) trace of
    │                             the loop running for one day
    └── example-diff.md        — what the proposed-improvements output
                                  looks like

Install story:
$ gh repo clone hriosnl/cc-starter-kit
$ cd your-project
$ ../cc-starter-kit/install.sh
installing cc-starter-kit into ./
  ✓ CLAUDE.md (review before committing)
  ✓ .claude/skills/reflect-on-session.md
  ✓ .claude/skills/propose-improvements.md
  ✓ .claude/skills/distill-memory.md
  ✓ .claude/hooks/stop.sh
next:
  1. read ./CLAUDE.md — it's a template, make it yours
  2. read ./docs/first-week.md
  3. start a session. the reflection loop will run at session end.
done.

What the end-of-session reflection looks like to the user (what the hook actually produces):
$ claude
(session ends)
...
reflection complete. 3 suggestions for your setup:

  [1/3] CLAUDE.md — add "test runner is vitest, not jest"
        reason: this came up twice in session and i had to guess
        [a]pply  [e]dit  [s]kip  [v]iew diff  >  a
        ✓ applied

        reason: when you say "migrate the schema", i don't have a
                checklist to follow. here's a draft one you can edit:
                (shows proposed skill content)
        [a]pply  [e]dit  [s]kip  [v]iew  >  e

  [3/3] docs/conventions.md — update: "imports use path aliases"
        reason: you corrected me on this 3 times in session. locking it in.
        [a]pply  [e]dit  [s]kip  [v]iew diff  >  a
        ✓ applied

3/3 reviewed. 2 applied.
setup compounded. good session.

This is the money shot. A reader sees this and immediately understands the whole thesis: the setup compounds, session by session, with your review at every step. No autonomy risk, no black box, visible value, almost nothing to learn.
What this is not: a framework Hiro has to maintain. It is a design-engineered starter, the way Tailwind UI is a starter. Users fork it and make it theirs. If someone wants to maintain a framework version, let someone else. Hiro stays the author of the original recipe.
Realistic build time: 3 weeks of design-engineer work, on Hiro’s own schedule, using Claude Code to do most of the actual coding. This is exactly the kind of project he’s built for.

Not a library with a semver contract.

Not a conference talk. Not a podcast. Not a Twitter-growth play.

_os/product/thesis.content:
This is a rough sketch of the first real thing that could come out of the vault. It is written for Hiro, to argue with. If any part of it doesn’t fit, kill it.
The core bet: Hiro’s edge is taste and philosophy applied to the lived practice of running a personal AI assistant. The product is the writing, the templates, and the opinionated recipe — not a framework, library, or startup. See hiro-profile for why this framing instead of a more ambitious one.
The problem
Everyone running a personal AI setup in 2026 — whether on Claude Code, OpenClaw, Cursor, or anything adjacent — hits the same wall after the first week:

The assistant starts from near-zero on every new task.
You re-teach context, conventions, preferences, vocabulary, over and over.
You accumulate half-written CLAUDE.md files, stray skills, ad-hoc hooks, and a vague sense that your setup should be getting smarter over time but isn’t.
You know the primitives exist. You just don’t know how to hold them — what goes in memory, what goes in skills, what goes in hooks, what goes in project docs, and how they should relate.

What’s missing isn’t another framework. The primitives are already here. What’s missing is a design philosophy and a lived practice — somebody who has sat with the real running system for months, paid attention to what broke and what compounded, and written it down with enough taste that other people can copy the pattern.
Hiro has already been doing this in private. Kaizen Mechanism.md is the spec. CC - Foundational Setup Ideas.md is the philosophy. CC - Foundational Setup Checklist.md is the open questions. All that’s missing is the step where it gets written down carefully enough to hand to someone else.
The insight

“CC should learn from everything, but reason with only what has been distilled.”
— from CC - Foundational Setup Ideas.md

This one line is the thesis for the whole product. The personal AI assistant is not a tool that improves autonomously. It is a tool that distills, with human review at every step. The human’s job is not to instruct the assistant. It is to run a Kaizen loop over the assistant’s own behavior, keeping what compounds and deleting what doesn’t. The assistant’s job is to make that loop cheap and visible.
The product is the practice of doing this well, documented by someone whose taste is trustworthy. Not a library. Not a framework. A way of working that readers can copy.
This is the difference between “here is a React library” and “here is how to build React apps.” The second is more valuable for an earlier audience.
What v0 ships
Four pieces, in order of how much work they are and how soon they can exist:
1. The rendered vault (ships as soon as we decide)
Hiro’s vault, published as a navigable site. Wikilinks become hyperlinks. The graph is browsable. Readers walk through his mind in the order their curiosity takes them. This is the manifesto — not a distilled essay, but the whole thinking, visible in its rough, unfinished state. Part of the appeal is that it is unfinished. See prototype for the rendering approach.
Value: zero to Hiro (the content already exists), high to readers (nobody else is publishing design-engineer-grade AI-assistant thinking in raw form).
2. One flagship essay — “Clarity is the new limit” (1–2 weeks of work)
A single sharpened essay extracted from Evolving Clarity.md and AI-First.md, under Hiro’s name, published on his own domain or Substack. 1200 words, tight, quotable, designed to be shared. The line “the new limit is clarity” is the hook; the body is the lived proof.
Value: entry point for readers who would never open a vault. Produces the first 500 subscribers.
3. The CC Starter Kit (3–6 weeks of work)
An opinionated, free, downloadable bundle that lets another power user run a CC-shaped setup of their own. Concretely:

A CLAUDE.md template encoding Hiro’s canonical rules (the Writing rules, the H - Prime values translated into instructions, the Kaizen loop as a skill)
A minimal skill pack: reflect-on-session, propose-improvements, distill-memory, maybe 3 more
A hook script for Claude Code’s Stop event that runs the reflection prompt after each session and produces the list of suggested diffs Hiro described in Kaizen Mechanism.md
A small docs/ folder explaining the why for each piece — with internal links back to the original vault notes
A README with an “install in 60 seconds” path

It is not software Hiro has to maintain as infrastructure. It is a starter — something a reader forks, adopts, edits, and makes their own. Think of it the way Tailwind UI is a starter, not a framework.
Value: this is the thing that travels. Power users share starter kits. It’s also the piece with the most design-engineer work per unit, which is exactly the shape Hiro thrives in.
4. A paid tier (after traction)
Once the essay and the kit have found an audience, there are natural paid products:

A weekly/biweekly essay behind a 8–15/mo Substack paywall
A “pro” starter kit variant with more skills, templates, and walkthroughs — $49 one-time or subscription
Eventually: a book. Personal AI: A Design Philosophy. Could be self-published on Leanpub first, then a traditional deal if the audience is there.

Value: this is where the money shows up, but it’s dependent on the above two earning trust first. Do not lead with it.
Why this wins
Shippable by Hiro as he already is. No new skills. No new tools. The starter kit is design-engineer work — bundles, docs, opinionated defaults, clean aesthetics. The essay is writing. The vault site is publishing what already exists. Every piece of this project uses muscles Hiro already has, and none of it requires him to become a founder, a salesperson, or a public figure.
Unique at the taste + philosophy layer. Plenty of people are building AI tools. Almost nobody with real design taste is publicly writing the design philosophy for how to run one well. The taste gap is real. Maggie Appleton is the closest comparable, and she isn’t deep in personal-assistant setup specifically.
Compatible with the reserved profile. Writer-builders can stay text-only for years before they ever need to appear on a stage. The audience comes to them, not the other way around. This is the only money path from the vault that honors the Self-Observation.md reality of Hiro needing equanimity.
Builds on rather than against the ecosystem. OpenClaw, Claude Code, Cursor are the platforms. We ride on top of them, we teach their power users how to use them better, we become a beloved voice inside those communities. No zero-sum competition. The ecosystems want someone doing this work.
Slow → fast. The writer-builder model is slow until it isn’t. The first 6 months are quiet — 500 subscribers, a few hundred kit downloads. The next 12 months, if the taste is right, can compound into low-six-figures of recurring income and an audience big enough for a book advance, a sponsored newsletter, or an advisory retainer on Hiro’s own terms. No VC arc. No acqui-hire panic. No “what are we raising for.” Just work that travels.
Why not the other paths

Not a framework/library. OpenClaw and the agent ecosystems already own this layer. Competing there means losing.
Not consulting. hiro-profile section: no prior shipping credibility, wrong personality profile for sales. Covered.
Not a venture-backed company. Can’t honor the equanimity requirement. Would break Hiro before it funded him.
Not a product for non-technical users (the SaaC vision from Income Ideas.md). Too ambitious for v0, too far from the current audience, better as a v3 dream.

What this requires from Hiro
Minimum viable commitment, if he wanted to try it:

~2 days to decide if this framing feels right and push back on what doesn’t.
~1 week to let the vault be rendered and published, probably pseudonymously at first or under just “Hiro” with no last name.
~1 week to sharpen the flagship essay from existing notes.
~3 weeks to build the starter kit, which is exactly the kind of design-engineer project he already enjoys.

That’s roughly 6 weeks of actual work, spread across however many months he wants. No urgency. No outside money committed. If any of it starts feeling off, stop.
Zak’s role here
To set expectations up front: Zak wrote this folder as a thoughtful read, not a partnership offer. He’s heads-down on his own project (Forgeloop) and isn’t available to co-build, run GTM, or otherwise carry any of this forward operationally. The _os/ folder is an honest strategic read you can use as input — zero obligation in either direction. See from-zak for the full framing. If a smaller ask comes up later (a read on a draft, a second pair of eyes), the door stays cracked open for that.

_os/product/why.title: Why this, why now
_os/product/why.content:
A short market read, written to justify the thesis in thesis. Not a pitch deck. A set of observations that add up.
1. The AI-assistant layer is finally stable enough to have a design philosophy
Until late 2025, the personal-AI-assistant space moved too fast for design philosophies to stick. Every month a new primitive showed up (memory, then skills, then hooks, then MCP, then managed agents). Writing “how to run your assistant well” was like writing a Rails guide in 2005 — it would be wrong in 60 days.
That stopped being true in the last 6 months. Claude Code, Cursor, OpenClaw (steipete), and the agent layer in general have converged on a shared shape: memory + skills + hooks + project docs + a tool to review changes. The primitives are stable enough that it is finally worth writing down how to use them well rather than what they are.
Hiro’s vault was written during this exact window. Kaizen Mechanism.md, CC - Foundational Setup Ideas.md, and CC - Foundational Setup Checklist.md are all observations from somebody sitting with the stabilized primitives and asking design questions. That timing is not an accident, and it is the core of why this is publishable now and wasn’t publishable a year ago.
2. The gap is aesthetic, not technical
Every serious AI-devtools company in 2026 is chasing faster per-token output. Not one of them is publishing what a beautifully-run personal assistant looks like. The engineering layer is saturated. The taste layer is empty.
This is exactly the kind of gap a design engineer with first-principles writing closes. Compare:

Infrastructure layer (saturated): OpenClaw, Claude Code, Cursor, Cline, Aider, Continue, Codeium, Cognition, Block, etc. All competing on primitives.
Framework layer (crowded): LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, LangGraph, AutoGen. Fighting over abstractions.
UX/taste/philosophy layer (nearly empty): Maggie Appleton in adjacent territory, a few scattered essays on Substack, nothing systematic, no recognized voice for “how should this feel.”

The layer where Hiro’s edge lives is almost completely uncontested. It will not stay uncontested forever — within 12 months, somebody is going to become the Maggie Appleton of personal AI setups. The only question is who.
3. The audience exists and is under-served
Who reads this stuff?

Every power user of Claude Code / Cursor / OpenClaw who has a CLAUDE.md file they know is not as good as it could be. Somewhere between 50k and 500k people, conservatively, and growing fast.
Every design-curious engineer who reads Maggie Appleton, Gwern, Cortex, Nadia Asparouhova, Ness Labs.
Every AI product designer trying to figure out what personal AI interfaces should feel like. They are starving for opinionated voices.
Founders/PMs of AI-devtools companies who want to know what their power users actually think. They will subscribe, read every post, and quietly copy ideas. A few of them will reach out to the author for advisory conversations. This is not a bad thing — it is a feature.

The total addressable audience for a newsletter in this space is probably 10k–30k paid subscribers at maturity. At 8–15/mo that is roughly 1M–5M ARR. Not venture-scale, but life-changing for a solo writer. And a much larger free-tier audience on top of it.
4. The model has proven itself in adjacent territory
This business shape is not speculative. It has happened, repeatedly, in the last 5 years:

Maggie Appleton — essays + design commentary → a following that underwrites everything she does. Book coming.
Gwern — essays → Patreon → one of the most trusted voices on LLM research despite not being an academic.
Nadia Asparouhova / Nadia Eghbal — essays on open source → book deal (Working in Public) → foundation work.
Cortex (Rosano) — opinionated software + blog → consistent audience → small paid products that compound.
Robin Sloan — novelist-adjacent, essays + small tools + Substack → combined income much higher than either alone.
Ness Labs early era (Anne-Laure Le Cunff) — newsletter → membership → book → mainstream.

What these people share: slow start, aesthetic consistency, point of view, don’t-chase-the-feed, eventually unreasonable compounding. None of them did VC. Several of them went through visible low-income phases of 12–24 months before it got traction. Hiro’s profile maps onto this shape almost exactly.
The precedent is clear enough that the risk is not “will this work” but “will Hiro ship it.”
5. The timing is specifically good for Hiro
Three overlapping signals:

The vault just got pushed to GitHub yesterday (2026-04-13/14). It’s active. Hiro is currently in an open, thinking, not-yet-committed phase. The window for a friend to walk in and offer a reframe is right now, not in six months when a path is already set.
Claude Code and the wider agent ecosystem shipped their foundational primitives in the second half of 2025. The design philosophy for those primitives has not been written yet. First-mover advantage for the Maggie-Appleton-equivalent role is still open.
There is a personal urgency in Self-Observation.md — the “I need to decide to stop” entry, the entries about draining people. Whatever that is pointing at, it means Hiro is looking for a path that isn’t the one he’s on. This is the moment to offer a concrete one he can walk or reject on his own terms.

6. What’s not urgent

Venture funding. Irrelevant to this shape.
Competitive speed. The writer-builder race is won on taste, not calendar.
First-mover at the infrastructure layer. Someone else already won those (OpenClaw, Cursor, Claude Code).
Public visibility of Hiro specifically. The reserved profile is compatible with years of quiet writing under just a first name.

Bottom line
There is a well-understood, historically validated, aesthetically correct, financially meaningful, reserved-founder-compatible career shape that Hiro’s vault maps onto with unusual precision, and the window to step into it is now. That is not a strong claim. It is what the evidence in the vault and the evidence in the market add up to.
The risk is not that the model is wrong. It’s that Hiro does not want to do it. That is for him to decide — see from-zak.

_os/strategy/kill-list.title: What we're not building
_os/strategy/kill-list.content:
A list of things that look tempting from inside the vault but should be deliberately not built, with reasons. This document exists so that future-Hiro has a clear list to point at when the pull to build one of them shows up.
Things to park, not build
The Intent Negotiation Protocol
Email Evolution - Intent Negotiation.md is a genuinely interesting vision. It is also an infrastructure-layer product idea that would take years to ship and has no obvious first customer. It would require a full team, venture funding, and a lot of Hiro being public.
Verdict: essay material only. The idea itself is excellent and will make a great essay or two (maybe “what if email went away”), but do not try to turn it into software yet. Park it.
Agent Swarms as a framework
The vault has Agent Swarm.md and Agent Swarm Diagram.md. The space is crowded (CrewAI, LangGraph, AutoGen, Swarm from OpenAI). Hiro’s framing — “no orchestrator, claims-based task allocation” — is interesting but not differentiated enough to win a framework fight. And Hiro does not want to run a framework.
Verdict: maybe an essay once the main thing is running. No framework, no library. Park.
SaaC — Software as a Consequence
From Income Ideas.md, the “on-demand software for non-builders, built on OpenClaw” vision. Big, genuine, several years early, and explicitly built on someone else’s infrastructure. Not a v0 project. Possibly not a v3 project.
Verdict: keep in the vault, occasionally nod to it in essays. Do not try to build. Park.
A “better Obsidian” / a “better Claude Code”
Any time someone reads the vault and thinks “Hiro should build his own editor / his own agent / his own IDE” — the answer is no. Competing at the tool layer is a full-time job and Hiro has a different edge. Build on top of existing tools, always.
A dashboard / SaaS / control plane
Whenever the word “dashboard” enters a proposal, assume it’s the wrong product. The thing we’re making is a set of design-engineered files and written thinking, not a hosted control surface. Dashboards require ops, billing, support, uptime, and a whole role that Hiro shouldn’t hire for in the first year.
A consultancy
Already killed in hiro-profile and from-zak. Restating it here: no consulting arm, no implementation services, no enterprise calls. Not because it couldn’t eventually happen — but because it is the wrong first move. It burns the voice and requires a sales muscle Hiro does not currently have.
A Substack-only empire
Substack is a useful distribution surface, not a strategy. The work is the vault + the kit + the essays. Substack is one channel among several. Never fall into the trap of writing to the Substack discovery algorithm instead of to the imagined reader in positioning.
A course
Courses look like a natural revenue path for this audience, and they are, but they eat enormous production time and require a product-development cycle (students, feedback, iteration, refunds) that would distract from the writing. If a course ever happens, it happens after the book, not before.
A VC round
Permanently off the table unless the business actually grows into something that obviously needs capital, which this shape likely won’t. VC is a specific tool for a specific kind of business, and this business is not that kind. Saying no early and often keeps the psychology clean.
Things to stop thinking about until v0 ships
This list is different from “park” — these are mental distractions that should be paused.

Long-term monetization architecture. (“Should the paid tier be 8 or 15? Annual or monthly? Bundle or unbundle?“) Irrelevant until there are 100 free subscribers.
Logo design, brand color systems. Irrelevant until the content is strong enough to carry.
Exit planning, acquihire possibilities. Irrelevant until the project exists.
Any conversation about “scaling the team.” One person ships v0. Maybe two. That’s the scope.
Any research into “where could I apply for an AI residency / grant / fellowship” as a substitute for shipping. Fellowships are a form of not-shipping.
Comparing this to whatever just trended on Hacker News. The pace is slow → fast. Compare only to the imagined reader in positioning.

The hard rule

No new notes until the first essay is published and the starter kit repo exists.

This is the rule Hiro should consider imposing on himself if he accepts any of this framing. The vault has enough raw material for a year of essays and three generations of the kit. What it does not have is shipped work. The constraint that matters is not ideation; it’s conversion of ideation into public artifacts.
Exceptions to the rule: Self-Observation.md and any journaling. Those are not “notes,” they are health infrastructure. Keep writing them.

_os/strategy/naming.title: Naming
_os/strategy/naming.content:
Three naming problems to sort out before anything ships publicly. Hiro gets the final call on all three — this is a starting list, not a decision.
1. The CC problem
CC is sacred and private. 90_Definitions/CC.md makes it clear: C.C. from Code Geass is the reference, and Hiro’s AI assistant is personal to him at a level that should not be productized. Taking the name public would flatten it. The rule we’re proposing is:

CC is Hiro’s private name for his personal AI assistant. It does not appear on the public site, in the kit, in essays, or in any marketing. Anywhere that the public-facing thing needs a name, we use a different one.

This is strictly about naming. The design that CC embodies — the Kaizen loop, the canonical rules, the distillation philosophy — can absolutely be written about and shared, because those are ideas, not the name.
When the vault is rendered for public reading, references to “CC” remain in the raw notes (Hiro’s private language). Public-facing files in _os/ use “the kit,” “the practice,” “the recipe,” or the name of whatever we choose in §2 below.
2. The starter kit needs a name
The thing described in prototype needs to be called something. It will be a GitHub repo, a download, possibly a paid product. Considerations:

Must not collide with CC, OpenClaw, Claude Code, Cursor.
Should be short (1–2 syllables preferred).
Should gesture at craft, compounding, or sharpening — not at automation, speed, or agents.
Should sound good next to Hiro’s voice. Not corporate, not cute, not meme-adjacent.
Should be ownable as a domain and on GitHub.

Starting options (for Hiro to pick from, reject, or use as a launching point):






































































CandidateMeaningFeelHonesharpen a blade by repeated usecraft, compounding, patient, calmKilnwhere raw material gets fired into formslow, transformative, design-adjacentForgeshaping metal through repeated workwarmer than kiln, more activeSmithythe workshop, not the smithplace-based, workshop vibeAnvilthe surface things get shaped ongrounded, specific, object-not-processWhetstonesharpens other toolssecondary but essential, humblePractice (the word itself)the thing itselftoo generic unless taken ironicallyCadencethe rhythm of the loopmatches Hiro’s “rhythm skill” noteDistillfrom the CC-Foundational-Setup linelifted from his own languageCompoundwhat the loop does over timefinancial overtone may be wrongKeelthe part that keeps a ship stable under loadmetaphorical, quietSetup (ironic)the most boring possible name, might workanti-branding branding
My personal gut ranking (totally overridable): Hone > Kiln > Whetstone > Cadence > Keel > others.
Reasoning for Hone: it’s a verb and a noun, it describes what the loop does (sharpens a working setup through repetition), it’s one syllable, it’s calm, it’s unclaimed in this space, and it pairs well with sentences like “notes on honing a personal AI setup” and “hone: an opinionated starter kit for personal AI assistants.”
3. The public site needs a name (or a non-name)
The rendered vault needs a URL. Three options in descending order of reservation:

hiro.xyz (or hiro.[something]) — just “Hiro.” First name only, no surname, no bio. This matches his reserved profile most closely and is the easiest to defend if someone asks “why no last name” (“I just like it like this”). Requires finding an available variant.
hiro-os.xyz or hiros-os.xyz — leans into the “Hiro OS” framing Zak coined. More descriptive, slightly less quiet, still low-profile.
[kit-name].dev or [kit-name].page — foreground the kit, background the person. Maximum reservation, but loses the personal-notebook feel that is a lot of the charm.

Recommendation: go with just hiro.* (first-name-only) for the vault and [kit-name].dev (or just github.com/hriosnl/[kit-name]) for the kit. Two separate URLs, one for the notebook, one for the artifact.
What gets named when

Now: Hiro picks his preferred kit name from the list (or rejects all of them and proposes his own). Everything else can wait.
Before the vault is rendered publicly: decide whether the site goes under just “Hiro” or whether a pseudonym feels better.
Before the flagship essay is published: decide the author byline. “Hiro” or a pseudonym. This is a one-way decision — pick the one Hiro feels he can keep.
Before the first paid product: everything has to have its final name. No more placeholders.

What not to do

Do not call anything “Hiro’s [thing].” That’s ownable language, but it doesn’t travel.
Do not use “CC” publicly anywhere, ever.
Do not pick a name that sounds like another AI framework. “Auto-[anything]”, “Agent-[anything]”, “Claude-[anything]”, “GPT-[anything]” — all out.
Do not pick a name that requires explanation. If the name needs a paragraph of etymology, pick a different name.
Do not pick a name that feels like Hiro was trying too hard. The whole positioning is “quiet and trustworthy” — a name that feels labored undercuts that immediately.
