_os/strategy/positioning.title: Positioning
_os/strategy/positioning.content:
A one-page positioning document. How we describe this, to ourselves and eventually to the world.
Category
“Design philosophy and lived practice for running a personal AI assistant.”
Not an agent framework. Not a developer tool. Not productivity software. Something adjacent to all three and built on top of them — the taste layer above the infrastructure layer. Think the way Maggie Appleton is “a designer who writes about digital gardens and AI” rather than “a note-taking product.” Her category is herself, and the product is the thinking.
The one-line

“Notes on how to run a personal AI assistant well — from somebody who runs one.”

That’s the Substack bio, the OG description, the landing page subhead, the one-line in Hiro’s GitHub profile. It should be this exact sentence until there’s a clear reason to change it.
The target reader
A single imagined reader, clear enough to write to:

A design-minded engineer or PM, probably mid-career, who has installed Claude Code or Cursor or OpenClaw and written their own CLAUDE.md file. They are good at their job and suspect their setup could be much better, but every blog post they find on the topic is either a changelog, a tutorial, or AI-generated. They want to read somebody’s taste, not somebody’s framework. They follow Maggie Appleton and Gwern. They keep meaning to read more Christopher Alexander. They are probably between 27 and 42. They don’t tweet much.

Everything we publish is written to this person. If a paragraph wouldn’t land for them, it doesn’t ship.
The wedge

“I am the person who has been sitting with a running personal AI assistant for months, paying attention, and writing down what I notice.”

The wedge is not expertise — expertise is cheap in this space. It is sustained, aesthetic, honest attention over time. Writing as field report. Claims grounded in a setup that actually runs. Nobody else is credibly doing this in public. Hiro’s vault is already the proof, because it was written privately with no audience to perform for.
What we are not

Not an agent framework (OpenClaw, Claude Code, LangGraph own this)
Not an IDE or editor (Cursor, Zed, VS Code own this)
Not a prompting library (crowded race-to-the-bottom)
Not a productivity course (wrong audience, wrong tone)
Not a consultancy (see hiro-profile — wrong profile)
Not a VC-funded startup (see why and from-zak — wrong shape)
Not an influencer brand (Hiro is reserved, and anyway the work should speak)
Not a “second brain” tool (Tiago Forte owns that category and the frame is wrong for this)

Every time we’re tempted to become one of these, we remember: the category is taste, not product. The asset is the writing, not the software.
The tone

First-person, second-person, present tense. Hiro’s 100_Canonical/Writing.md already codifies this. Stay there.
Short sentences with occasional long ones for rhythm.
Specific, not abstract. When there’s a choice between a general principle and a specific anecdote from the running setup, always pick the anecdote. The voice earns authority by being lived.
No name-dropping. No “as Andrej Karpathy said.” The work doesn’t need to borrow credibility from anyone else.
No hedging filler. Strike “I think that maybe perhaps” everywhere. Hiro’s H - Prime explicitly values first-principles directness. Honor it.
Quotable by default. Every 400 words, at least one sentence that a reader would screenshot. This is not a stylistic flourish — it’s how writing like this actually spreads.

The visual brand

Minimal. Serif or monospace headline. Dark-on-light default, readable dark mode.
One column. Wide margins.
No hero images.
Generous whitespace.
Occasional hand-drawn or Excalidraw diagrams where they help — Hiro is a design engineer, let his taste show.
No stock illustrations. No emoji logos. No rainbow gradients.
The whole thing should feel like somebody’s notebook, not a product.

The reference aesthetic: gwern.net, maggieappleton.com, obsidian.md’s own docs, escapingflatland.substack.com, overreacted.io.
The audience size we’re aiming for

Year 1: 1,000 free subscribers, 100 paid (8–15/mo), ~50 kit downloads/month. Small, real, trusting.
Year 2: 5,000 free, 500 paid, book proposal in motion, 1–2 advisory conversations/quarter on Hiro’s own terms. First year of living income.
Year 3: 15,000+ free, 1,500+ paid, book out, kit has a polished pro version, modest sponsorship revenue, inbound that includes “come work here” offers from the right companies (decline most).

These numbers are modest by venture standards and life-changing at an individual level. The trajectory is slow → fast, not fast → flatline. The writer-builder model requires patience.
Distribution strategy

Substack for the newsletter — not because it’s the best tool, but because it has the right audience for this exact shape.
Own domain for the vault and the kit landing page. Do not let the platform own the canonical URL.
GitHub for the starter kit. It is a design-engineer-shaped artifact and GitHub is where design engineers live.
Hacker News for launches, carefully, no more than once a quarter, and only with finished work.
Cross-post to @hiro on X if at all, with minimal effort. Do not try to win on Twitter. The audience finds us through links, not feeds.
Lurk in OpenClaw / Claude Code communities but do not pitch. Answer questions. Share the kit when it’s genuinely useful. Be the person whose replies people remember.

Risks to the positioning

Sounding precious or overwritten. Guard against this by keeping every essay grounded in something that actually happened in a real session.
Being mistaken for a framework. Say “recipe” and “starter kit” and “practice” and “notes.” Never say “platform” or “framework.”
Losing the reserved profile by accident. If any essay or piece of copy reads as performative, rewrite it. Hiro’s edge dies if the voice stops feeling honest.
Getting pulled into the competitive frame by readers who want this to be OpenClaw vs. Claude Code vs. Cursor drama. Refuse the drama politely. Write about the practice, not the tools.

00_Legacy/CSS-for-JS-developers.title: CSS for JS developers
00_Legacy/CSS-for-JS-developers.content:
Box-sizing the hell out of it
Instead of having to remember to swap box-sizing on every layout element, we can set it as the default value for all elements with this handy code snippet:
\*, \*::before, \*::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
It’s super important that you never apply the following CSS, removing the outline:
button {   outline: none; }
Margins
It’s easy to fall into the trap of thinking that margin is exclusively about changing the selected element’s position. Really, though, it’s about changing the gap between elements.
Negative margins can take some element out of its parent container
Directions in Flow Layout
Block elements don’t share
Inline elements can line-wrap
Height and Width
Broadly speaking, there are two kinds of values we can specify for width:

Measurements (100%, 200px, 5rem)
Keywords (auto, fit-content)

width default is auto, while height is close to min-content
height tends to look “down” the tree, to determine its size based on the natural size of its contents, while width tends to look “up” the tree, basing its size on the space made available by the parent.
Margin Collapse
Margin collapse is unique to Flow layout. If you have children inside a display: flex parent, those children’s margins will never collapse.
Margins must be touching in order for them to collapse.

Positioned Layout
The defining feature of positioned layout is that items can overlap. The Flow Layout algorithm tries very hard to make sure that multiple elements never occupy the same pixels.
Position: relative -  relative to its natural position.

Constrains certain children
Enables additional CSS properties to be used.

Unlike margins, position doesn’t impact layout.
relative positioning can be applied to both block and inline elements.
Position: absolute
Absolutely-positioned elements are adjusted based on their container, not based on their in-flow position.
When we set something to be position: absolute, we pull it out of flow.
Absolutely positioned elements are strictly compliant.
Containing Blocks
A containing block is a rectangle that forms the bounds of the element’s container.
Absolute elements can only be contained by other elements using Positioned layout
padding is used in Flow layout calculations, and absolute elements are taken out-of-flow. Those rules don’t apply.
Stacking Contexts
As a general rule, positioned elements will always render on top of non-positioned ones. We can think of it as a two-stage process: first, all of the non-positioned elements are rendered (everything using Flow, Flexbox, Grid…). Next, all of the positioned elements are rendered on top (relative, absolute, fixed, sticky).
z-index only works with positioned elements. It will have no effect on an element being rendered in Flow layout.
The isolation property
Instead of adding position: relative; z-index: 1; to our .pricing selector, we can do this:
.pricing {
isolation: isolate;
}
The isolation property does precisely 1 thing: creates a stacking context.
Fixed Positioning
If a parent or grandparent uses the transform property, it becomes the containing block for the fixed element, essentially transforming it into an absolutely-positioned element or transformed parents can’t have fixed children.
Also, the will-change: transform declaration has the same effect
Overflow
overflow: auto is the ideal behaviour when we know an element might overflow
Adding detailed comments when using overflow: hidden is absolutely critical. Otherwise, you’ll never remember why you set the property.
Horizontal Overflow
white-space is a property that lets us tweak how words and other inline/inline-block elements wrap. By setting it to nowrap, we instruct the container to never break lines. That, in tandem with overflow: auto, allows us to achieve a horizontally-scrollable element.
Sticky Positioning
An often-overlooked aspect of position: sticky is that the element will never follow the scroll outside of its parent container. Sticky elements only stick while their container is in view.
Sticky elements are like relative or static elements in this regard; they’re laid out in-flow. They take up real space, and that space remains taken even when the element is stuck to an edge during scrolling.

Flexbox
align-self - for secondary/cross axis
in a flexbox, width and height are hypothetical, flexbox does not respect it when there is no space left—but there’s a minimum width and height, and that probably is the text content
flex-basis, the size of the dimension in main axis i.e. width or height
flex-grow overrides flex-basis
flex-shrink and flex-grow defines how fast the element should shrink or grow
There are two important sizes when dealing with Flexbox: the minimum content size, and the hypothetical size.
flex-basis can’t scale an element below its minimum content size, but width can
Use the flex shorthand, e.g. flex: 1 0 500px;
combine flex-wrap: wrap with flex-basis (and max-width)
Content vs Item
Content - the whole group
Item - the individual item
Positioned Flex children
When there is a conflict between layout modes, positioned layout always wins.
Relative position is compatible, the element will be laid out first as flex item then positioning (top, left, etc)

Animation
transform: scale, scale even the descendants unlike changing the width and height
This reveals an important truth about transforms: elements are flattened into a texture

grid-template-rows: 1fr 1fr

Custom commands 🔗
To create a custom command, you need to set up a specific folder structure in your project:

Find the .claude folder in your project directory
Create a new directory called commands inside it
Create a new markdown file with your desired command name (like audit.md)
The filename becomes your command name - so audit.md creates the /audit command.

Custom commands can accept arguments using the $ARGUMENTS placeholder.
MCP Servers
Allow all Playwright tools:
{ "permissions": { 	”allow”: [“mcp__playwright”],
"deny": [] } }
Hooks

Here’s the confusing part:

The stdin input to your commands will change based upon the type of hook being executed (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Notification, etc)
The tool_input contained in that will differ based upon the tool that was called (in the case of PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks)

To handle this challenge, it is recommended to use a hook like this:
"PostToolUse": [ // Or "PreToolUse" or "Stop", etc
  {
    "matcher": "*",
    "hooks": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "jq . > post-log.json"
      }
    ]
  },
]
Notice the provided command. It will write the input to this hook to the post-log.json file, which allows you to inspect exactly what would have been fed into your command! This makes it a lot easier for you to understand what data your command should inspect.

You might have expected a more sophisticated solution, but I think it’s worth showing that sometimes solutions like this one also give you the expected results. I do this often when I’m prototyping something to save time.

Performance

✅ The rule of thumb here is that you should try to animate with transform and opacity as they only trigger the third rendering step (composite) while padding or margin triggers all three.
Transforms don’t trigger layout recalculation as they only affect the visual representation of an element, not its position in the document flow.
The problem with JS animations arises when they are using requestAnimationFrame to animate. Javascript code will always run on the main thread. This means that if the browser is busy doing something else, it might skip a frame, causing the animation to drop frames.
 Framer Motion is using requestAnimationFrame (calculates in the main thread)
Personally, I often times combine CSS animations with Framer Motion. CSS for simple animations and those that should be hardware-accelerated, and Framer Motion for more complex/sophisticated animations.
❌ Once the content of the drawer got bigger than ~20 list items the drag gesture became laggy, and I couldn’t figure out why. Dragging was done without any re-renders, so what could cause it to drop frames? Every time the drag position gets updated, I changed a CSS variable which is then used as the value for translateY().

Since CSS Variables are inheritable, changing them will cause style recalculation for all children, meaning the more items I have in my drawer, the more expensive the calculation gets. Updating the style directly on the element fixed the issue. This seems like a quick fix in retrospect, but it took me hours to figure out.




Custom component note: When using popLayout mode, any immediate child of AnimatePresence that’s a custom component must be wrapped in React’s forwardRef function, forwarding the provided ref to the DOM node you wish to pop out of the layout.

The designer does not, as a rule, begin with some preconceived idea. Rather, the idea is (or should be) the result of careful study and observation, and the design a product of that idea.
The designer is primarily confronted with three classes of material:

a) the given material: product, copy, slogan, logotype, format, media, production process;
b) the formal material: space, contrast, proportion, harmony, rhythm, repetition, line, mass, shape, color, weight, volume, value, texture;
c) the psychological material: visual perception and optical illusion problems, the spectators’ instincts, intuitions, and emotions as well as the designer’s own needs.

Because advertising art, in the end, deals with the spectator, and because it is the function of advertising to influence him, it follows that the designer’s problem is twofold:

to anticipate the spectator’s reactions and

Perfect Asian Fried Rice
Start with rice made at least a few hours before that you dry out in the fridge (or on the countertop if you live in a desert like me). Type of rice doesn’t particularly matter unless you pick some weird stuff like basmati or brown rice that’s not supposed to become fried rice. Always wash your rice, Chinese style rice is not supposed to be gooey or sticky but rather dry.
Heat wok up to max, add splash of high temp oil and coat inside surface, then immediately throw in your eggs and vigorously scramble/fry with a pinch of salt. Set aside.
Use thawed vegetables, stir fry like above w/max heat and generous splash of oil immediately before adding ingredients. Add more durable veggies like carrot before delicate veggies or aromatics like onion or garlic. At max heat it should only need a minute or two of full blast cooking before you add your rice and spices. Fry until texture is satisfactory, then turn off heat and allow it to cool a bit before adding soy sauce. Soy sauce should cook on lower heat because it can easily burn and turn bitter if you’re not careful.
You must always be tossing and turning your ingredients over extremely high heat to get that restaurant flavor you’re looking for. The key is to always keep heat high and moisture low to avoid boiling your ingredients - this is why you cannot use frozen veggies. Chinese stir frying is 90% preparation of ingredients; you do not have time to mess with getting stuff out of the fridge or cutting/peeling ingredients. Get it all organized onto a plate before you start, your final result will reflect this effort.
